ⓐ.summary: The decline in crime in the United States is closely related to lead exposure, mediated by a 20-year time lag from childhood exposure.

c1.text: Violent and property crime in the US entered a sharp declining trend from the early 1990s, continuing until 2020.

c2.text: Claim ⓐ: The decline in crime in the United States is closely related to lead exposure.

c3.text: From post-WWII until the early 1970s, an increase in lead emissions from cars was followed by a rise in violent crime.

c4.text: After lead began to be removed from gasoline in the 1970s, violent crime subsequently decreased.

c5.text: Rates of violent and property crime are highest in the late teens to early twenties.

c6.text: In children, unlike adolescents or adults, exposure to lead affects brain development and induces increased aggression and impulsivity, affecting future potential for criminal behavior.

c7.text: The effect of childhood lead exposure on crime emerges with an approximately 20-year time lag when affected children reach their late teens or early twenties.

h1.text: The average blood lead levels of American children aged 1–5 in 2000 had dropped to half the level of 1990.

h2.text: The drop in childhood lead levels in 2000 accounts for the continued crime decline through 2020 via the 20-year time lag.

a.note: The drop in childhood lead levels in 2000 explains the ongoing crime decline through 2020 via the 20-year lag, strengthening ⓐ.

h3.text: The sharp decline in violent crime in the US began in the 1990s rather than the 1970s.

h4.text: The decline in crime in the United States is not closely related to lead exposure.

b.note: The naive inference rb1 (decline in 1990s rather than 1970s means lead was not the cause) is undercut by c7: the ~20-year time lag.

h5.text: Adolescents in the United States who committed crimes had four times the bone lead content of those who did not.

h6.text: There is a positive correlation between lead exposure and criminal behavior.

c.note: Higher bone lead content in adolescent offenders supports a positive correlation between lead exposure and criminal behavior, strengthening ⓐ.
